papers.title: Hesperetin Modulates the PINK1/Parkin-Mediated Mitophagy Pathway to Alleviate Cognitive Deficits and Mitochondrial Dysfunction in a Rat Model of Alzheimer's Disease.
papers.summary: This study investigates whether hesperetin, a flavonoid compound, can improve cognitive function in a rat model of Alzheimer's disease. The researchers found that hesperetin works by activating the PINK1/Parkin mitophagy pathway, which is the cellular process for clearing damaged mitochondria. The treatment appeared to reduce mitochondrial dysfunction and improve cognitive deficits in the affected rats.
papers.why: This paper provides direct evidence on PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy in a neurodegenerative disease model, offering mechanistic insight and a potential pharmacological modulator relevant to the mitophagy focus of the PhD project, though it lacks the spatial transcriptomics/metabolomics or interneuron-specific angle.

papers.title: Chaperone-mediated autophagy targets Miro-1 for degradation to promote mitophagy and inhibit α-synuclein induced ferroptosis.
papers.summary: This paper studies how a specific type of autophagy called chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA) helps clear out a protein called Miro-1 from damaged mitochondria. Removing Miro-1 allows the cell to properly tag and recycle these damaged mitochondria through a process called mitophagy. The study shows that this clearance process can protect neurons from a harmful form of cell death (ferroptosis) triggered by the protein α-synuclein, which is heavily implicated in Parkinson's disease.
papers.why: This work directly addresses a core mechanistic link between chaperone-mediated autophagy and mitophagy in neurons, which is central to understanding neuronal quality-control pathways relevant to the PhD project's focus on mitophagy and autophagy in the brain.
papers.figure: A figure showing the proposed model/pathway linking CMA-mediated Miro-1 degradation, mitophagy induction, and reduced ferroptosis upon α-synuclein expression.

papers.title: CASTLE: Cell-type aware SpaTial domain detection via contrastive learning embedding.
papers.summary: CASTLE is a computational method designed to identify spatial domains in tissue by combining cell-type information with contrastive learning to create meaningful embeddings. It aims to improve upon existing spatial domain detection tools by making the representations more aware of underlying cell-type identities rather than treating spatial spots generically. This approach could enhance the accuracy of segmenting tissue regions based on both spatial organization and cellular composition.
papers.why: This method could help delineate spatial domains enriched for specific interneuron subtypes or perineuronal net-associated regions in brain tissue, improving the resolution of spatial transcriptomics analyses relevant to the PhD project.
papers.figure: Figure showing the model architecture and comparison of spatial domain detection accuracy against benchmark methods on brain tissue datasets.

papers.title: Unified cell segmentation for spatial transcriptomics via transcript reassignment
papers.summary: This paper presents a computational method for unifying cell segmentation results in spatial transcriptomics data by reassigning transcripts across overlapping or inconsistent segmentation boundaries. The approach aims to resolve discrepancies between different segmentation algorithms or imaging modalities, producing a single consistent cell map. This improves accuracy in assigning individual RNA transcripts to the correct cells, which is foundational for downstream single-cell analyses.
papers.why: Accurate cell segmentation and transcript assignment is essential for reliably mapping gene expression to specific neurons, interneurons, and perineuronal net-associated cells in spatial transcriptomics studies of mitophagy and autophagy in the brain.
papers.figure: Figure showing example segmentation overlays comparing raw vs. unified transcript reassignment across cell boundaries.

papers.title: Scalable, unsupervised, and annotation-free discovery of cell–cell communication modules across 2D and 3D spatial omics with STARComm
papers.summary: STARComm is a new computational method for analyzing spatial omics data that automatically identifies patterns of communication between neighboring cells without requiring pre-existing cell-type labels or manual annotation. It works across both 2D and 3D spatial datasets and is designed to scale efficiently to large, complex tissue samples. By treating cell-cell communication as modular units discovered directly from the data, it bypasses traditional annotation bottlenecks and could reveal novel interaction patterns in tissue microenvironments.
papers.why: This tool could help map how neurons, interneurons, and the cells maintaining perineuronal nets communicate spatially within brain tissue, directly supporting spatial transcriptomics/metabolomics analyses central to this PhD project.

papers.title: Sphinx: An R package for adaptive spatial neighborhood modeling and functional analysis in spatial omics.
papers.summary: Sphinx is a newly introduced R package designed to analyze spatial omics data by modeling adaptive spatial neighborhoods around cells or spots. It allows researchers to functionally interpret spatial relationships, such as how nearby cells influence each other's gene expression or molecular profiles. This tool aims to improve the detection of spatially-driven biological patterns in complex tissue datasets.
papers.why: This tool could help analyze spatial transcriptomics and metabolomics data around neurons and perineuronal nets by modeling how spatial neighborhoods influence gene expression and metabolic patterns in brain tissue.

papers.title: LUCID: joint cell typing and neighbour-aware decontamination of segmented spatial transcriptomics
papers.summary: LUCID is a computational method designed to improve spatial transcriptomics analysis by jointly performing cell type assignment and correcting for signal contamination from neighboring cells. In segmented spatial transcriptomics data, transcripts from densely packed cells can be misassigned to the wrong cell boundaries, muddying gene expression profiles. LUCID tackles this by modeling cell identity and neighbor-based decontamination together, aiming to yield cleaner, more accurate single-cell spatial transcriptomic data.
papers.why: Accurate spatial transcriptomics with proper decontamination is essential for reliably distinguishing interneuron subtypes and their spatial transcriptional signatures in densely packed brain tissue, which is central to this PhD project's spatial transcriptomics and interneuron focus.

papers.title: Acute nicotine exposure produces a spatially organized transcriptional response in mouse olfactory cortex
papers.summary: This study examines how a single acute dose of nicotine affects gene expression patterns across the mouse olfactory cortex. Using spatial transcriptomics, the researchers mapped where and how different cell populations respond transcriptionally to nicotine exposure. They found that the transcriptional response is not uniform but organized spatially within the cortical architecture.
papers.why: Although focused on olfactory cortex and nicotine rather than mitophagy, this paper demonstrates spatial transcriptomics methodology for mapping region-specific transcriptional responses in brain tissue, which is directly relevant to the analytical approaches used in the PhD project.
